zh.q: 干手、湿手都是同一只手，为什么湿了反而容易触电？
zh.concl: 人的手上常会沾有 NaCl（汗液的成分之一），当遇到水时形成电解质溶液；电解质溶液能够导电，所以湿手直接接触电源时容易发生触电事故（教材原话）。
points: 三只杯子里有两只是对照：蒸馏水与 0.10 mol/L NaCl 溶液，中间那只是「待测样品」。
电流表是唯一能把「有没有导电」变成数的仪器（分度 1 mA）。
湿手的危险不在水，在水把汗里的盐变成了能自由移动的离子。

zh.q: 一勺干燥的 NaCl 固体，为什么接上电源电流表一动不动？
zh.concl: 能导电的物质必须具有能自由移动的、带电荷的粒子；干燥的 NaCl 固体里 Na⁺ 与 Cl⁻ 紧密排列、不能自由移动，受热熔化后产生能自由移动的离子（教材原话）。
points: 「干燥固体不导电」不等于「NaCl 不是电解质」——电解质看的是水溶液里或熔融状态下能不能导电。
熔融也导电，说明离子本来就在晶体里，只是被束缚住了。
熔融读 25 mA 是被 60 Ω 限流电阻压进量程的，熔体本身导电能力比溶液强得多。

zh.q: 同一勺 NaCl，加水搅一搅就导电了，水做了什么？
zh.concl: 电解质溶于水或受热熔化时，形成自由移动的离子的过程叫做电离；水分子把 Na⁺、Cl⁻ 从晶体表面拉下来，成为能自由移动的水合离子（教材原话）。
points: 电离是溶解（或熔化）时自动发生的，不需要通电（教材练习 2 的 D 项就错在这里）。
溶液与熔体都导电，但离子的来源不同：一个靠水分子拉开，一个靠加热克服作用力。
电离方程式用等号（强电解质），离子符号就是溶液里实际存在的粒子。

zh.q: 蒸馏水是水，蔗糖溶液也是液体，为什么都测不出电流？
zh.concl: 电解质必须是化合物，且在水溶液里或熔融状态下能导电；蔗糖溶于水不电离，溶液里没有自由移动的离子，所以不导电。
points: 「能导电」不是电解质的判据——铜丝、石墨都导电，但它们是单质。
「溶于水」也不够——蔗糖溶得很好，一点电流也没有。
蒸馏水那一格的 0 是「这套装置测不出」，不是「绝对不导电」（教材脚注专门交代）。

zh.q: 都是 0.10 mol/L 的一元酸，盐酸 21 mA、醋酸只有 1 mA，差在哪？
zh.concl: 相同物质的量浓度的盐酸和醋酸的 pH、导电能力都有差别，说明两种酸中 H⁺ 浓度不同，即电离程度不同：HCl 全部电离，CH₃COOH 只有部分电离（教材原话）。
points: （选必1 内容）比较两种电解质「谁导电强」必须同浓度、同温度——否则比的是浓度不是强弱。
（选必1 内容）弱电解质的电离是可逆的，写可逆号；它的溶液里分子与离子同时存在。
（选必1 内容）「强电解质的导电能力一定更强」是错的：极稀的盐酸可以比很浓的醋酸弱（教材练习 5（1））。

zh.q: 往 Ba(OH)₂ 溶液里一滴滴加稀硫酸，电流为什么会先降到 0 再回升？
zh.concl: SO₄²⁻ 与 Ba²⁺ 发生反应，生成难溶的 BaSO₄ 白色沉淀；电解质在溶液中的反应实质上是离子之间的反应（教材原话）。
points: 电流下降不是「电池没电了」，是能自由移动的离子被沉淀带走。
最低点在 10.0 mL：Ba²⁺ 与 OH⁻ 刚好够和滴进来的 H⁺、SO₄²⁻ 完全反应。
最低点不是「没有反应」，恰恰是「反应刚好做完了」——导电能力约为 0 说明溶液里几乎没有自由移动的离子（教材题 9 ②）。

zh.q: 电流归零的那一刻，杯子里到底还剩什么？
zh.concl: 带正电荷的水合钠离子向与电源负极相连的电极移动，带负电荷的水合氯离子向与电源正极相连的电极移动；SO₄²⁻ 与 Ba²⁺ 结合生成难溶的 BaSO₄ 白色沉淀（教材原话）。
points: 离子只在溶液里移动，电子只在导线里移动，两条路不串。
阳离子去负极侧、阴离子去正极侧——两个方向相反，别看反。
沉淀不是「消失了」，是以白色固体沉在杯底；溶液里能动的离子少了，电流就小了。

zh.q: 如果把稀硫酸换成稀盐酸，那条「先降后升」的曲线还会有吗？
zh.concl: 复分解反应发生的条件之一是生成沉淀：Ba²⁺ 与 SO₄²⁻ 生成难溶的 BaSO₄；换成盐酸时只发生中和，离子数没有减少，只是体积变大被稀释。
points: （课件加的对照，教材未做）「先降后升」的形状来自 BaSO₄ 沉淀带走离子，不是来自「中和」本身。
中和只把 H⁺ 与 OH⁻ 变成水；换成盐酸时 Ba²⁺、Cl⁻ 还在，导电能力只降一点。
教材题 9 的 ③ 项说 BC 段靠过量 Ba(OH)₂ 导电，是错的——恰好反应后过量的是酸。

zh.q: 考核：把稀硫酸滴到「恰好完全反应」那一点
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：恰好完全反应时，溶液里的 Ba²⁺ 与 OH⁻ 刚好被滴进来的 SO₄²⁻ 与 H⁺ 用完，自由移动的离子最少，导电能力最低。
points: 找最低点就是找「离子最少」的那一点，电流表比看沉淀更灵敏。
滴定剂必须是稀硫酸——换成盐酸不会有最低点，钩子在这里。
体积只差 0.5 mL，电流就差好几 mA，所以滑块步长是 0.5 mL，达标窗口留了 ±0.5 mL（两个步长）。

en.q: Dry hand or wet hand, it's the same hand. Why is a wet one more likely to get a shock?
en.concl: Hands often carry NaCl (one component of sweat), which forms an electrolyte solution with water; electrolyte solutions conduct, so touching a power source with wet hands easily causes a shock (textbook wording).
points: Two of the three beakers are controls, distilled water and 0.10 mol/L NaCl solution; the middle one is the "test sample".
The ammeter is the only instrument that turns "does it conduct" into a number (1 mA divisions).
The danger of wet hands isn't the water itself; water turns the salt in sweat into freely moving ions.

en.q: Why doesn't the ammeter move at all with a spoonful of dry NaCl solid connected?
en.concl: A conducting substance must have freely moving charged particles; in dry NaCl solid, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are tightly packed and can't move freely, and melting produces freely moving ions (textbook wording).
points: "The dry solid doesn't conduct" doesn't mean "NaCl isn't an electrolyte": electrolytes are judged by conducting in aqueous solution or when molten.
The melt conducts too, showing the ions were in the crystal all along, just held in place.
The molten reading of 25 mA is held within range by the 60 Ω limiting resistor; the melt itself conducts far better than the solution.

en.q: Add water to the same spoonful of NaCl and stir, and it conducts. What did the water do?
en.concl: When an electrolyte dissolves in water or melts, the process of forming freely moving ions is called ionization; water molecules pull Na⁺ and Cl⁻ off the crystal surface as freely moving hydrated ions (textbook wording).
points: Ionization happens on its own when dissolving (or melting); it doesn't need current (option D of textbook exercise 2 gets this wrong).
Both the solution and the melt conduct, but the ions come about differently: water molecules pull them apart in one, heat overcomes the attractions in the other.
Ionization equations use an equals sign (strong electrolytes), and the ion symbols are the particles actually present in solution.

en.q: Distilled water is water, and sucrose solution is a liquid too. Why does neither give a current?
en.concl: An electrolyte must be a compound that conducts in aqueous solution or when molten; sucrose doesn't ionize in water, so its solution has no freely moving ions and doesn't conduct.
points: "Conducts" isn't the test for an electrolyte: copper wire and graphite conduct, but they're elements.
"Dissolves in water" isn't enough either: sucrose dissolves well and gives no current at all.
The 0 for distilled water means "this setup can't detect it", not "it doesn't conduct at all" (the textbook footnote points this out).

en.q: Both are 0.10 mol/L monoprotic acids, yet hydrochloric acid gives 21 mA and acetic acid only 1 mA. What's the difference?
en.concl: Hydrochloric acid and acetic acid at the same molar concentration differ in pH and conductivity, showing their H⁺ concentrations, and so their degrees of ionization, differ: HCl ionizes completely, CH₃COOH only partly (textbook wording).
points: (Selective Book 1 content) Comparing "which electrolyte conducts better" requires the same concentration and temperature; otherwise you're comparing concentrations, not strength.
(Selective Book 1 content) Weak electrolyte ionization is reversible and written with a reversible arrow; its solution contains both molecules and ions.
(Selective Book 1 content) "A strong electrolyte always conducts better" is wrong: very dilute hydrochloric acid can conduct worse than very concentrated acetic acid (textbook exercise 5(1)).

en.q: Adding dilute sulfuric acid drop by drop to Ba(OH)₂ solution, why does the current fall to 0 and then rise again?
en.concl: SO₄²⁻ reacts with Ba²⁺ to form a sparingly soluble white BaSO₄ precipitate; reactions of electrolytes in solution are essentially reactions between ions (textbook wording).
points: The falling current isn't "the battery running down"; freely moving ions are being carried off by the precipitate.
The minimum is at 10.0 mL: Ba²⁺ and OH⁻ are just enough to react completely with the H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ added.
The minimum isn't "no reaction"; it's precisely "the reaction has just finished". Conductivity near 0 means there are almost no freely moving ions left (textbook question 9 ②).

en.q: At the moment the current hits zero, what's actually left in the beaker?
en.concl: Positively charged hydrated sodium ions move toward the electrode connected to the negative terminal, and negatively charged hydrated chloride ions toward the electrode connected to the positive terminal; SO₄²⁻ and Ba²⁺ combine into a sparingly soluble white BaSO₄ precipitate (textbook wording).
points: Ions move only in the solution and electrons only in the wire; the two paths never cross.
Cations go to the negative side, anions to the positive side, in opposite directions; don't swap them.
The precipitate hasn't "disappeared"; it settles as a white solid at the bottom. With fewer mobile ions in solution, the current drops.

en.q: If dilute sulfuric acid is replaced with dilute hydrochloric acid, is there still a "fall then rise" curve?
en.concl: One condition for a double displacement reaction is forming a precipitate: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ form sparingly soluble BaSO₄; with hydrochloric acid only neutralization occurs, the number of ions doesn't fall, and the volume just increases and dilutes it.
points: (A control added by this lesson, not in the textbook) The "fall then rise" shape comes from BaSO₄ precipitation removing ions, not from "neutralization" itself.
Neutralization only turns H⁺ and OH⁻ into water; with hydrochloric acid, Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ remain, so conductivity drops only a little.
Item ③ of textbook question 9, saying segment BC conducts because of excess Ba(OH)₂, is wrong: after exact reaction, it's the acid that's in excess.

en.q: Assessment: add dilute sulfuric acid up to the point of "exact complete reaction"
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: at exact complete reaction, the Ba²⁺ and OH⁻ in solution are just used up by the added SO₄²⁻ and H⁺, freely moving ions are fewest, and conductivity is lowest.
points: Finding the minimum means finding the point with "fewest ions"; the ammeter is more sensitive than watching the precipitate.
The titrant must be dilute sulfuric acid; hydrochloric acid has no minimum. That's the catch here.
Just 0.5 mL off changes the current by several mA, so the slider step is 0.5 mL and the pass window is ±0.5 mL (two steps).
